text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London closed slightly lower in thin turnover unimpressed by the sharp rise in New York. Traders said while LIFFE's revised grading criteria had caused an increase in robusta supplies for the September position, ungraded coffees were still being hedged in the futures market.

It was added that even though there have been grading problems over the last couple of months, people are aware there are plenty of robustas around. September lost $1 to close at $1,644 per tonne, while November gave up $4 to close at $1,646 per tonne.

Arabica futures in New York ended sharply higher on concern about near-term supply tightness. Also forecasts of cooler weather in Brazil aided sentiment. The September/December switch widened to 32.55 cents compared with 30.30 cents at the close on Wednesday.

Some believe that the supply tightness is not real and simply manufactured by producers/exporters holding back in hopes of pushing the market up but that is not likely to be the case as ICO statistics show that producers have been shipping aggressively all season to take advantage of the higher prices.

Hence, it should not come as a surprise that supplies have become tight. Some traders expect September's hefty premium to December to attract coffee to the board. In all likelihood this is coffee held in European stocks rather than in producer hands. There were rumours that the GCA figures for July will show a rise.

Again much of the build in US stocks has been of robusta and Brazilian coffee not suitable for delivery to the Board. September added 8.25 cents/lb to close at 208.80 cents/lb, while December closed 6 cents/lb higher at 176.25 cents/lb.

ROTHFOS GMBH - World coffee production in 1997/98 could rise to 100.048 million 60-kg bags, up from 99.343 million bags produced in 1996/97 and 86.981 million bags produced in 1995/96 figures from German trade house Bernard Rothfos GmbH show.

Rothfos said American milds in 1997/98 should account for 34.070 million bags, showing a 1.98 million bag increase over the 1996/97 figure of 32.095 million bags. African and Asian milds output should also increase due to better East African crops, with 7.261 million bags targeted for 1997/98 after 6.518 million bags in 1996/97. Unwashed arabica crops should be down at 24.600 million bags in 1997/98 from 28.600 million bags in 1996/97, mostly due to a lower Brazilian crop.

Brazilian arabica production in 1997/98 is forecast to fall to 20 million bags, down from 24.0 million bags the previous year and 12.8 million bags produced in 1995/96. Robusta production in 1997/98 is forecast to reach 5.0 million bags, unchanged from last year but above the 3.0 million bags produced in 1995/96, Rothfos said.
World robusta production in 1997/98 is forecast at 34.117 million bags compared with 32.130 million bags produced the previous year, with a recovery in Indonesian output cited as one reason.

Global coffee consumption in 1997/98 is forecast at 101 million bags, rounded, compared with 99.6 million bags in 1996/97. The 1997/98 figure is made up of 76.0 million bags forecast to be consumed in importing countries and just under 25 million bags likely to be consumed in producer countries.

The 1996/97 figure consists of a 24.1 million bag estimate of consumption in producing countries, which was unchanged from a May estimate although prices in producing countries had risen, and a 75.5 million bag estimate for importing countries' use. The latter figure was up from an estimated 75 million bag consumption figure envisaged for 1996/97 in May and compared with an identical 75 million bag figure given for 1995/96.

The exportable crop in 1997/98 was pegged at 75.06 million bags, little changed from 75.21 million bags in 1996/97, which Rothfos said 'indicates the delicate balance which continues to exist between production and disappearance levels.'
UNITED STATES - The CSCE reported certified coffee stocks fell by 1,530 bags as of August 6 to 90,929 bags. An additional 3,218 bags were pending grading, the exchange said.

AUSTRALIA - Australia imported 77,041 bags of coffee in June 1997, nearly 10 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1997 up to 448,400 bags, 2 per cent less than was imported the same period in 1996.

Total imports in calendar year 1996 rose by 3.7 per cent to 845,200 bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/June 1997 were Vietnam (133,400 vs 126,000 bags) and Papua New Guinea (113,600 vs 128,000 bags).
